lead: A list of vectors is linearly independent when the only way to combine them into the zero vector is to multiply every vector by zero. That one test decides whether a spanning set carries spare vectors, whether a coordinate list is unique, and whether two solutions of a differential equation are really different. Independence is the check behind basis, dimension and rank, and it is used wherever a system must have one answer and not many.
prereq: You need: linear combinations from chapter 2.3, and row reduction from Unit 1, Gaussian elimination.

sections.h3: The only combination that gives zero

blocks.text: V is a vector space over a field F — take F = R or F = C, as in chapter 2.1. A set S = {v₁, v₂, …, vₖ} of vectors in V is linearly independent when
c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + ⋯ + cₖvₖ = 0  ⟹  c₁ = c₂ = ⋯ = cₖ = 0
blocks.where: v₁ … vₖ are vectors in V; c₁ … cₖ are scalars from F; 0 on the right is the zero vector of V, not the number zero.

blocks.text: If some scalars, not all zero, add up to the zero vector, then S is linearly dependent, and that choice of scalars is a non-trivial relation.
The zero choice always works: 0v₁ + ⋯ + 0vₖ = 0. Independence says nothing else works. Dependence says something else does.

Dependence has a second face. Suppose c₁ ≠ 0 in a non-trivial relation. Then v₁ = −(c₂/c₁)v₂ − ⋯ − (cₖ/c₁)vₖ, so v₁ is a linear combination of the other members (chapter 2.3). A dependent set has at least one vector that the rest already span. That vector is spare.
Say "a linearly independent set of vectors", as most syllabi do. Independence belongs to the set, not to one vector on its own.

sections.h3: Facts you can prove in one line

items: Zero vector. Any set containing 0 is dependent, because 1·0 + 0v₂ + ⋯ + 0vₖ = 0 with coefficient 1 ≠ 0.
Subsets. A subset of an independent set is independent. Pad any relation on the subset with zeros for the missing vectors; the large set has only the trivial relation, so the small one does too.
Supersets. A superset of a dependent set is dependent. Keep the non-trivial relation and give every new vector the coefficient 0.
Two vectors. {u, v} is dependent exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other: u = λv gives 1·u − λ·v = 0; and au + bv = 0 with a ≠ 0 gives u = −(b/a)v.

Rⁿ. Any n + 1 vectors in Rⁿ are dependent. Write a homogeneous system with n equations and n + 1 unknowns; more unknowns than equations leaves a free variable, so a non-zero solution exists (see Unit 1, Gaussian elimination). That solution is a non-trivial relation among the columns.

blocks.text: For three or more vectors, "no vector is a multiple of another" proves nothing. In R³ the vectors (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (1, 1, 0) have no such multiple, yet the third is the sum of the first two, so the set is dependent.
To test v₁, …, vₖ in Rⁿ, make them the columns of a matrix A with k columns, then row reduce it (Unit 1). S is independent exactly when every column of A is a pivot column, that is, when rank A = k.

Why it works: a column without a pivot is a free variable, so Ax = 0 has a non-zero solution x, and x is a non-trivial relation among the columns. Chapter 2.6 reads the same test through the null space. Row operations change the columns but keep the relations between them, so the pivot count is safe to read off the reduced matrix.
Square case: n vectors in Rⁿ are independent exactly when det A ≠ 0, because rank n means A is invertible.

Functions are vectors too (chapter 2.1). Two solutions y₁, y₂ of a linear homogeneous differential equation are independent functions when the Wronskian W(x) = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂ is not identically zero. For solutions of a second-order equation with continuous coefficients, one point x₀ with W(x₀) ≠ 0 settles independence, and then W is never zero on that interval.

figure.caption: The second vector is exactly twice the first, so the combination in the last row reaches the zero vector without every coefficient being zero. That is a dependence, found by eye and then confirmed by the pivot test.

spec.title: A relation found by inspection, then checked
spec.aria: The second vector is twice the first, so a non-zero combination of the three vectors gives the zero vector.

examples.question: In R³ take v₁ = (1, 2, 3), v₂ = (2, 4, 6), v₃ = (1, 0, 1). (a) Show that {v₁, v₂, v₃} is dependent by giving a non-trivial relation. (b) Show that {v₁, v₃} is independent. (c) Confirm both answers with the pivot test.
steps: Move everything to one side: 2v₁ − v₂ + 0v₃ = (2, 4, 6) − (2, 4, 6) + (0, 0, 0) = (0, 0, 0). The coefficient 2 is not zero, so the set is dependent. The scalars are c₁ = 2, c₂ = −1, c₃ = 0.
(b) Let a v₁ + b v₃ = (0, 0, 0). In coordinates: a + b = 0, 2a = 0, 3a + b = 0.
The second equation gives 2a = 0, so a = 0.
The first equation then gives b = 0. The third holds: 3(0) + 0 = 0.
Only the trivial solution exists, so {v₁, v₃} is independent.
(c) Columns v₁, v₂, v₃ give A = [[1, 2, 1], [2, 4, 0], [3, 6, 1]]. R2 − 2R1 gives (0, 0, −2); R3 − 3R1 gives (0, 0, −2). Pivots sit in columns 1 and 3 only, so rank A = 2 < 3: dependent.
Columns v₁, v₃ give B = [[1, 1], [2, 0], [3, 1]]. R2 − 2R1 gives (0, −2); R3 − 3R1 gives (0, −2). Both columns hold a pivot, so rank B = 2 = the number of vectors: independent.
examples.answer: The set {v₁, v₂, v₃} is dependent, with relation 2v₁ − v₂ + 0v₃ = 0; the set {v₁, v₃} is independent; the pivot counts are rank A = 2 and rank B = 2.
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction

def rank(rows):
    M = [[Fraction(x) for x in r] for r in rows]
    m, n = len(M), len(M[0])
    r = 0
    for c in range(n):
        piv = None
        for i in range(r, m):
            if M[i][c] != 0:
                piv = i
                break
        if piv is None:
            continue
        M[r], M[piv] = M[piv], M[r]
        pv = M[r][c]
        M[r] = [x / pv for x in M[r]]
        for i in range(m):
            if i != r and M[i][c] != 0:
                f = M[i][c]
                M[i] = [a - f * b for a, b in zip(M[i], M[r])]
        r += 1
    return r

v1 = [1, 2, 3]
v2 = [2, 4, 6]
v3 = [1, 0, 1]

A = [list(col) for col in zip(v1, v2, v3)]
B = [list(col) for col in zip(v1, v3)]
print(rank(A))
print(rank(B))

c = [2, -1, 0]
comb = [c[0]*v1[i] + c[1]*v2[i] + c[2]*v3[i] for i in range(3)]
assert comb == [0, 0, 0]
print(c[0])
print(c[1])
print(c[2])

traps: One failed attempt at finding a relation proves nothing. Independence needs a proof from the equations, not a hunch that no relation exists.
The field matters. {1, i} is independent over R but dependent over C, because i·1 − 1·i = 0 uses the scalar i. Check which field the question uses.
"No vector is a scalar multiple of another" decides only the two-vector case. With three vectors you must test all combinations, as (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (1, 1, 0) shows.
A set containing the zero vector is always dependent, and a set listing the same vector twice is always dependent; examiners ask for both as one-mark parts.
Independent is not the same as orthogonal, and dependent is not the same as parallel in a picture. Independence is about coefficients, not about angles.

quiz.q: State the definition of a linearly independent set of vectors in a vector space V over a field F.
quiz.a: The set {v₁, …, vₖ} is independent when c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₖvₖ = 0 with cᵢ in F forces c₁ = ⋯ = cₖ = 0.

quiz.q: Why is any set that contains the zero vector automatically dependent?
quiz.a: Give the zero vector the coefficient 1 and every other vector the coefficient 0. The sum is the zero vector and a coefficient is non-zero, so a non-trivial relation exists.
Add the first two: (1, 1, 0) + (0, 1, 1) = (1, 2, 1), which is the third. So v₁ + v₂ − v₃ = 0 with coefficients 1, 1, −1, not all zero. The set is dependent.
Solve a(1, 2) + b(2, 5) = (0, 0): a + 2b = 0 and 2a + 5b = 0. From the first, a = −2b; the second gives −4b + 5b = 0, so b = 0 and a = 0. Independent, and det [[1, 2], [2, 5]] = 5 − 4 = 1 ≠ 0 agrees.

quiz.q: If {v₁, v₂, v₃} is independent, show that {v₁ + v₂, v₂ + v₃, v₁ + v₃} is independent.
quiz.a: Let a(v₁ + v₂) + b(v₂ + v₃) + c(v₁ + v₃) = 0. Collect terms: (a + c)v₁ + (a + b)v₂ + (b + c)v₃ = 0. Independence of {v₁, v₂, v₃} gives a + c = 0, a + b = 0, b + c = 0. Subtract the last two to get a − c = 0; with a + c = 0 this forces a = 0, then b = 0 and c = 0. So the new set is independent.

quiz.q: Why are any n + 1 vectors in Rⁿ dependent, but n vectors may be independent?
quiz.a: The relation c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₙ₊₁vₙ₊₁ = 0 is a homogeneous system of n equations in n + 1 unknowns. There are more unknowns than equations, so a free variable remains and a non-zero solution exists — a non-trivial relation. With n vectors the pivot count can reach n, and then only the zero solution exists.

quiz.q: A student sets three vectors as columns of A, row reduces, and finds two pivots. What does that say about the three vectors, and about the null space of A?
quiz.a: Two pivots among three columns means rank A = 2 < 3, so the three vectors are dependent. One free variable remains, so the null space has dimension 1 and holds a non-zero vector x with Ax = 0 — a non-trivial relation among the columns.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same test runs over other fields: independence over the two-element field underlies error-correcting codes and network coding, where a dependent set of packets cannot be recovered. Independence axioms stripped of coordinates give matroids, the object behind greedy algorithms for spanning trees and scheduling. In signal processing, compressed sensing asks when a few columns of a wide random matrix stay independent, so a sparse signal can be recovered from few measurements. Numerically, near-dependence is measured by singular values rather than exact pivots, which is where Unit 5, SVD, takes over. Search for matroid, spark of a matrix, and Wronskian to go further.
